title: Teaching Trump (and Other Controversial Topics) Without Losing Your Job
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart tells the story of showing a one-sided Ezra Klein video about Donald Trump in his history classes, drawing a parent complaint to his principal, and responding with a written explanation and apology. He treats the episode as his own failure of even-handedness and builds from it a three-part framework for teaching controversial topics. The first imperative is to be as even-handed as possible, drawing on Gerald Graff's warning that students who feel browbeaten learn only that school is where you are told what to think. The second is to explicitly teach argument, and the third is to let students actually argue, with Pop-Up Debate as a management structure. He closes by arguing that teaching controversy is core to educating for a democratic society, with the aim being a good decision rather than victory.
points: Stuart models professional humility by owning a real lapse, including lopsided evidence, and the way he and the school resolved it graciously.
Even-handedness is about the evidence set a teacher provides, not just what the teacher says, since students detect lopsided sources.
One-sided argument removes student autonomy and therefore motivation, so bias undermines the very critical thinking the lesson targets.
Argument has to be taught explicitly (for example with argument-builder templates) and then practiced under structured, civil classroom-management protocols.
Fulkerson's aim of argument, a good decision where everyone risks changing their view, gives teachers a standard to hold up for students.
quotes: As it turned out, later that night a parent called my principal, concerned about me “pushing my politics” on students through showing the video. My principal spoke with me the next day, and I submitted a written explanation of why I shared the video along with an apology.
All of that is to say that I made a mistake, primarily in the area of even-handedness (the First Imperative — see below). And the point of this article is to help you do better than me.
we’ll be teaching them that school is a place where they’re told what to think. Inevitably, this demotivates kids. There’s no autonomy in a one-sided argument.

The Second Imperative is that we must actually teach students to argue. Much has been written on this, but the simplest starting places I’ve found are the “Argument Builder” sheets produced by Les Lynn over at Argument-Centered Education.

Here, classroom management is critical, and I recommend the Pop-Up Debate protocol as a management tool. The goal during a debate on a controversial topic is that everyone participates, that an atmosphere of intellectual engagement is maintained throughout the argument, and that respect and civility are the behavioral norms.
Teaching the controversies, to me, isn’t an optional teacher thrill; it’s not the sky diving of teaching. Rather, it’s a central part of the educator’s work in maintaining a democratic society.
